paragraphs.text: A cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from [Yiwu](greater-yiwu:where-it-is), made in 2004 and kept since in Guangzhou’s tea trade. The area lies in the north of Mengla County, in Xishuangbanna, and counts among the old Six Famous Tea Mountains; its town has long been where leaf from the surrounding villages is gathered and processed.

The leaf was fried in a wok to [kill the green](sheng:making), then rolled and dried in the sun, never by hot air. That leaves some of the leaf’s own activity alive, which is why a cake like this keeps changing for years after it is pressed.

At twenty-two years it has passed the twenty that many in the trade wait for before calling raw pu’er [aged](sheng:ageing), though some count from ten. Because the tea changes through slow oxidation and the work of microbes, heat and humidity set the pace, so its years in [storage](sheng:storage) shape it as much as the date does.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
